Inside the D.S.A.’s Audacious Quest for Power in the Democratic Party
This summer, I traveled to several states, talking to candidates, organizers and voters to try to understand the origins of the growing democratic socialist movement.

Members of the Democratic Socialists of America, the country’s largest socialist organization, are eager to discuss the failures of mainstream Democrats, who are increasingly out of step with voters on issues from Israel to data centers.
But some factions within the D.S.A. are conflicted about its growing relationship with the Democratic Party, even if it intends to use that party for its own ends.

Democratic voters are conflicted, too. The democratic socialist candidate Francesca Hong narrowly lost in the Wisconsin governor’s race this week, failing to overcome the opposition of the state’s establishment.

Across the country, I felt as if I was watching an extraordinary shift in the boundaries of Democratic politics. This has implications for the 2028 presidential race, where there is anticipation about the prospect of a D.S.A. candidate.
